I am seventy-eight years old, and these bones have worked this land for fifty-five years. My wife and I are the only ones left in the household, so we must be careful not to bite off more than we can chew. We have 4.1 mu total, and I know every inch of it.

I keep about 3 mu in our wheat-maize rotation. That is our rice bowl. The wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does. Now that spring is starting, I will top-dress it with urea when it greens up, and irrigate from our well three times before harvest—at green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. I will spray twice for aphids and rust. I use improved wheat seeds that have done well here for years; I do not buy hybrid wheat seed because it is costly and unnecessary on our small plot. I apply about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu over the season, plus 5 kg each of phosphorus and potassium in the compound fertilizer. I expect around 450 kg of wheat per mu if the weather holds.

After we cut the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. We rotary-till quickly and plant summer maize that same week. For maize, I always buy hybrid seed. That is one expense I do not skip; the yield difference is too big. I put down compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress with urea when the maize is knee-high. We irrigate three times—our well never fails us—and spray twice for borers. I hope for 550 kg per mu of maize.

The remaining 1.1 mu is for cotton. Cotton is our cash crop. I will plough that field deep in late April because cotton roots need loose soil. I plant improved Bt cotton seed to save on pesticide for bollworms, but I still spray three times for aphids and spider mites. I apply less fertilizer to cotton than to grain—about 12 kg nitrogen per mu, plus 5 kg phosphorus and 6 kg potassium—and irrigate three times, especially at flowering and boll-setting. Picking cotton is hard on the back, but 1.1 mu is just enough for us to handle. I expect about 250 kg of seed cotton per mu.

At my age, I do not chase the highest possible yield. I aim for steady, manageable harvests that do not break our backs or our wallet. Too much fertilizer makes plants lush but sick; too many sprays waste money. We will eat some grain, sell the rest, and sell the cotton to the buyer who comes to the village. That is how we live.
